item.title: Introduction
item.description:
info

Status vex v0.0.0, in development.

vex is the embeddable, local-first, markdown-based task system. Every task is a plain-text markdown file with YAML frontmatter, and every project keeps its own .vex folder, much like a .git folder. There is no server, no daemon and no account.

Because a task is a text file, anything that reads and writes text can work with it: your editor, a shell script, or an AI coding agent.

item.title: CLI reference
item.description:
Conventions link

vex <command> [arguments] [--flags]

  • Every word up to the first --flag is positional. add and recipe join them into the description.
  • [focus] is optional everywhere. Without it, a command uses your saved focus (prev). See Focuses.
  • --field value sets a field; a --field without a value names one.
  • Quoting works as in a shell: --vexbody "two words" is one value, and --filter status:"not done" matches not done.
  • A comma outside quotes makes a list: --children a,b sets two children, and vex focus a,b focuses on both tasks. A value containing spaces keeps its commas, and \, writes a literal comma.

Commands link

Command Description
vex help [command] Lists every command, or describes one.
vex init Creates a .vex folder in the current folder.
vex add Description [--fields...] Creates and resolves a task, prints its vexid and focuses on it.
vex show [focus] Prints each task’s frontmatter and body.
vex get [focus] [row_sep] [col_sep] [--fields...] Prints one tab-separated line per task. --select a,b names the fields as a list. Defaults to vexid. A row separator and a column separator replace the newline and tab (see

item.title: Configuring vex (config.lua)
item.description:
.vex/config.lua returns a Lua table and is read on every command. vex init writes this one:

 return {
 taskfolder = '.',
 default = {
 tasktype = 'task'
 },
 taskowners = {},
 loglimit = 1000,
 paths = {
 groupby = {'status', 'lineage'}
 }
}

This repository’s own config sets taskfolder = "vexdoc/vex": its backlog is the vex folder of this wiki.

Settings link

Setting Effect
taskfolder The folder, relative to the project root, that holds the task files.
taskowners The names owner may take. With no task owners, tasks can’t have an owner.
default.tasktype The vextype of a task added without one.
paths.groupby Nests task files in folders by their fields (see below).
loglimit How many lines the verb and event logs in .vex/vexdex keep (see

item.title: Configuring views
item.description:
Each .lua file in .vex/views can register views. A view is a display function that takes the focus and the command’s flags and returns the text to print:

 view:view 'count' {
 display = function(focus, flags)
 return #focus:get() .. ' tasks'
 end
}
 
vex view all count

focus:get() returns the focus’s tasks. Read any field from them, transients included. Flags arrive as a table: vex view all count --field status gives flags.field == 'status'.

item.title: Creating your first task using vex
item.description:
This page walks through the core loop: init, add, show, set, get, focus, resolve and remove.

1. Initialise a project link

cd my-project
vex init

Task files go in the folder named by taskfolder in .vex/config.lua. By default that’s the project root (see Configuring vex (config.lua)).

item.title: Frontmatter schema
item.description:
Every task is validated against the schema of its vextype and of each type that type extends (see Task types (and vexations)). This page lists the fields vex defines. Any other field you set is stored as given.

Fields on every task link

Field Type Description
vexid text Unique id and filename, generated from the description when the task is added. It can’t be changed.
description text Required. At least 2 words and more than 3 characters.
vextype text The task type. Defaults to task and must be a registered type.
status state todo, then done. vex rejects any other move. Defaults to todo. Abstracts store none: it is worked out from their children (

item.title: Configuring task types
item.description:
Each .lua file in .vex/tasks can register task types and transients.

Task types link

A type extends an existing one and adds a schema. Its tasks must pass its own schema and every ancestor’s:

 task:task 'bug':extends 'atom' {
 schema = schema.atleast {
 severity = schema.any {'low', 'high'},
 reported = schema.maybe {schema.formatted {schema.datetime}},
 }
}
 
vex add Crash on start --vextype bug --severity high

A schema validates, normalises, derives and converts a task’s fields each time it is resolved. Build yours from these blocks, among others:

item.title: Task types (and vexations)
item.description:
Every task has a vextype. The base type is task. The vexations plugin adds four types on top of it, each answering a different question about the work. Every type keeps all of task’s fields (see Frontmatter schema).

vextype Answers Body Structure
exploration What do I need to know? Empty No children
abstract What needs to happen? Empty children: the tasks it groups
decision Which path do we take? Free options, and a decision from among them
atom What do I actually do? Free No children

Exploration link

Use an exploration when you don’t yet know what needs to happen. The task marks an open question. The exploring itself happens in your notes or an outliner, so the body stays empty.

item.title: Using a recipe to create a sequence of tasks
item.description:
A recipe is a named shortcut that creates one or more tasks with fields already filled in. Use one whenever you set up the same kind of work repeatedly.

Listing recipes link

vex recipe
Available recipes:
 abstract

With no name, vex recipe lists the recipes available. vex ships abstract, which creates a task of type abstract: a parent that groups other tasks.

item.title: Configuring recipes
item.description:
Each .lua file in .vex/recipes can register recipes. A recipe is an add function that receives the task manager and the properties from the command line, and adds tasks:

 recipe:recipe 'chore' {
 add = function(task, taskproperties)
 taskproperties.vextype = 'atom'
 return {task:add(taskproperties)}
 end
}
 
vex recipe chore Take out the bins

taskproperties holds the description and every flag. add returns the list of vexids it added. A recipe can add as many tasks as it likes and link them through their fields; vex resolves and writes each returned task in the order of the list, then focuses on all of them:

item.title: Views
item.description:
A view renders the tasks in a focus:

 vex view [focus] [view]

With no arguments, vex view lists the views. With one argument, it is the view, rendering the saved focus. Views show the fields each task stores. A focus built with --select shows only the selected fields, transients included.

tabular link

A table of every field except the body, formatted for reading. A list shows as its comma-separated values, and a field a task doesn’t have is left blank. To fit a terminal, every cell and header is cut to 40 characters, ending in ...; a list is cut between its values.

item.title: Configuring focuses
item.description:
Each .lua file in .vex/focuses can register named focuses. A named focus is a function that returns a list of tasks, usually built from other focuses:

 focus.register_focus('mine', function()
 return focus.focus('all'):filter('owner', 'alice'):filter('status', 'done'):get()
end)
 
vex focus mine --select due
vex view mine kanban

A named focus works wherever a focus does (see

item.title: Getting into focus
item.description:
A focus is a saved query over your tasks. vex focus builds one and most other commands act on it. CLI reference > Focuses describes every flag.

Cheatsheet link

Command Does
vex focus <start> [--flags...] Builds a focus from a starting point, applies the flags in order and saves it.
vex focus --flags... Applies the flags to the saved focus.
vex focus Prints the saved focus.
vex get, show, set, resolve, remove, view With no focus given, act on the saved focus.
vex view <start> <view> [--flags...] Renders a focus without saving it.
Flag Keeps
--filter field:value Tasks where field equals value.
--fuzzy field:value[:n] Tasks where field contains value, give or take n typos.
--between field:low:high Tasks where field is in the range. Either end may be empty.
--nil field Tasks with no value for field.
--select a,b Only those fields.
--orderby field[:desc] Tasks sorted by those fields.
--groupby field Tasks in groups. Later flags work per group.
--rn Numbers each group’s tasks from 1.
--first n, --last n The first or last n tasks, per group after --groupby. Order them with --orderby first.
--step field The tasks one hop along field: children, forwardlinks, backlinks.
--tree field, --reversetree field The tasks plus everything reachable from, or reaching, them through field.
--union, --intersect, --xor, --notin, --onlyin, --complement Set operations.

item.title: Configuring event hooks
item.description:
Each .lua file in .vex/events can register hooks. Every event comes in a pair: pre-<event> fires before the action and post-<event> after it. For example, pre-verb-set fires before the vex set command runs, and post-task-resolve fires after a task resolves. A hook receives the event’s args (see the table below):

 event:on 'post-task-resolve' (function(vexid, t)
 if t.due and t.due < os.time() and t.phase ~= 'final' then
 print(vexid .. ' is overdue')
 end
end)

A hook that raises an error stops the command. vex prints which hook failed, on which event, and why, for example Event hook 'needs-owner' failed on 'pre-verb-set': .... A pre- hook can therefore enforce project rules before anything changes, for example requiring every task to have an owner:

item.title: Status and state machines
item.description:
A task’s status is todo or done, and only todo can move to done:

vex set tidy-readme-1 --status done
vex set tidy-readme-1 --status todo
ERROR: Cannot transition status from done to todo
...

Setting a task to its current status is fine, and doing is not a status: vex set --status doing fails with Cannot transition status from todo to doing.

item.title: Working with git and a team
item.description:
Tasks are plain text files, so git and vex work together with a little care.

What to commit link

Commit the task files in taskfolder, .vex/config.lua and your extensions (tasks, recipes, focuses, views, events).

Keep .vex/vexdex/ out of git by adding it to .gitignore. It holds the index, which vex rebuilds from the task files, and your saved focus, which is personal.

item.title: Links and backlinks
item.description:
A task links to another by holding its vexid in children, options, decision or dependencies. In the task file a link is written [[vexid]], so Obsidian draws the graph. vex checks every link when it resolves: the target must exist, a child has one parent, and dependencies can’t form a cycle.

Links as fields link

item.title: Errors and troubleshooting
item.description:
Every user mistake fails with a named error, a message and a hint, and exits non-zero. Internal error is the exception: that is a bug in vex, so please report it.

Errors link

Error Cause Fix
not-vexed No .vex folder in the current folder or above it. vex init, or cd into your project.
already-vexed vex init where a .vex already exists. Nothing to do.
no-focus A command needed the saved focus and there is none, or it can’t be replayed. vex focus <name> or vex add to set one.
unknown-focus The focus is not a named focus, a vexid in the index or a path. Check the spelling. If the task exists on disk, vex resolve all.
unknown-focus-operation A flag that isn’t a focus operation, such as --colour. See

item.title: Contributing
item.description: vex is a single LuaJIT program with no build step. This page covers working on it; Plugin architecture and Resolution pipeline explain how it fits together.

item.title: Design journal
item.description:
Philosophy link

Simple way to create and manage tasks, embeddable in any project, and local first.

Tasks are just folders and markdown files.

Focus on using the task management system to reduce uncertainty, make decisions, and create maximum efficiency sets of actionable items.

Philosophy is to be minimalist, creating first a CLI tool which could be expanded into other tools.

All written in luajit so it runs on a potato.

item.title: Events and hooks
item.description:
Events go through one event manager, src/lib/event.lua. They fire at two levels:

  • Verbs. lib.cli fires pre-verb-<verb> before every command runs and post-verb-<verb> after it finishes.
  • Actions. The task, focus, view and recipe managers fire pre- and post- events around each public action, such as pre-task-resolve or post-focus-write.

At the end of loading, vex runs every .lua file in .vex/events, sorted by path, and each file registers its handlers. Handlers run in the order they were registered. A handler that raises an error stops the command with a hook-failed error naming the hook and the event. See

item.title: Plugin architecture
item.description:
Every swappable part of vex, including id generation, file layout, the task file format and sort order, goes through one mechanism: src/lib/plugin.lua.

Enums: named slots with one active member link

Plugin:addenum(name, members, active) registers a slot: a name, the implementations that can fill it, and the one that is active. src/vex.lua registers six:

 plugin:addenum("tagger", {"canonicalvexid"})
plugin:addenum("taskpath", {"grouppath"})
plugin:addenum("taskformat", {"obsidian"})
plugin:addenum("sortdata", {"canonicalsort"})
plugin:addenum("frontmatter", {"canonicalfrontmatter"})
plugin:addenum("body", {"canonicalbody"})

Plugin:select(name, member) switches the active member. The rest of vex depends only on the slot. Markdown with YAML frontmatter is simply what the obsidian member of taskformat writes; another member could store the same fields as JSON or database rows, and schemas, focuses and views would work unchanged.

item.title: Resolution pipeline
item.description:
How a task goes from vex add to a file on disk, and what else moves when it does. The code is TaskManager in src/core/task.lua.

add, resolve, write link

  1. TaskManager:add makes a vexid with the tagger plugin and holds the new task in memory only.
  2. TaskManager:resolve runs the schema of the task’s type and of each type it extends, from the root down. Each schema runs three steps: normalise (fill defaults, convert values), validate, and derive (compute fields, record links). A failure throws a named resolution-failed-* error and nothing is written. Resolution then indexes the task in memory and moves files into place (below).
  3. TaskManager:write formats the task back to its readable form (a timestamp becomes YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS, a vexid becomes [[vexid]]), writes it through the taskformat plugin to a temporary file and renames it into place (

item.title: The index
item.description:
The vexdex (src/core/vexdex.lua) is vex’s index: a map from each vexid to its task data, kept in .vex/vexdex so that commands don’t read every task file on every run. It is derived entirely from the task files, so keep it out of git and rebuild it with vex resolve all.

On disk link

File Holds
index.bin Every task’s fields except the body, unformatted: timestamps as numbers, links as bare vexids. The body lives only in the task file, and a query on vexbody (or the overview’s body count) reads it from there.
backlinks.bin For every task, the tasks that link to it.
paths.bin Where each task file is, relative to taskfolder.
focus.bin The saved focus, as the list of operations that rebuild it.

Each .bin file is written with binser and is what vex reads. Next to it, a .lua file holds the same data in readable form. vex never reads the .lua files; they exist so you can inspect the index.
